Relative to a neutral macro communiqué, the September 2023 FOMC statement is a hawkish hold: policy remains restrictive at 5.25–5.50%, balance-sheet runoff continues, and the Committee stays “highly attentive” to inflation risks despite “solid” growth and low unemployment.

Incorporating the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS) tightens the overall tone. The July 2023 SLOOS indicates broad-based credit supply tightening and softer loan demand: banks tightened standards across commercial real estate and residential real estate (including GSE-eligible, government, QM/non-QM jumbos), as well as HELOCs, and tightened terms for credit card and auto loans, with notably weaker demand in subprime mortgages. These data corroborate the statement’s warning that tighter credit will weigh on activity and hiring and suggest a stronger drag from bank credit than a neutral read would imply. While the banking system is described as “sound and resilient,” SLOOS evidence of ongoing tightening tempers the modestly positive growth remarks and reinforces a risk-management bias.

Netting “solid” activity against persistent inflation concerns and SLOOS-confirmed credit headwinds, the assessment shifts closer to neutral and more cautious than before.
